data.title: Rekomberek – an L-shaped hillfort above Horné Orešany
data.excerpt: Above the Parná river near Horné Orešany lies the hillfort of Rekomberek, enclosed by an L-shaped rampart some 390 m long around an interior of 0.8 ha. It has never been officially excavated, yet the ground nearby yielded one of the most important Late Avar hoards known from Slovakia and Czechia — 86 objects, among them a bronze cross of Byzantine type.

children.text: The hillfort of Rekomberek (Rekomperk) lies in the cadastral area of the village of Horné Orešany above the course of the Parná river, roughly above the Husí stok spring, which is well known to walkers because a marked trail runs alongside it. The slopes of the Rekomperk hill are fairly steep, and its summit therefore offered a reasonably suitable position for a fortification that could be well defended. The fortification occupied the summit part of the hill and is bounded by a rampart built of earth and stone. In places the rampart is more clearly visible to the naked eye (above all in the southern part of the fortification) and in others it fades away. Lidar mapping, however, shows the whole course of the fortification very distinctly: it has roughly the shape of the letter L. Its total circumference is about 390 metres and the interior of the hillfort covers about 0.8 ha. The entrance gate into the hillfort lay on the southern side of the fortification. The hillfort measures about 140 metres along its longest axis, and inside it one can find quite level areas, ideal for living and for building dwellings.

No official archaeological excavation has taken place at the hillfort so far, and today it has in all likelihood been plundered by metal detectorists. Karol Pieta, in the paper in which he published the site, noted that according to his information bronze objects from the period of the Avar Khaganate had been found at the hillfort — probably therefore from the 8th to the early 9th century — which unfortunately are in a private collection, and their owner did not make them available to archaeologists for documentation. From the interior of the hillfort it was possible to document a hoard consisting of two coulters and one ploughshare, that is, objects that formed part of a plough in the Slavic period. These are typical objects of the Great Moravian period. A bronze earring was also found at the hillfort in the area of the entrance gate, typologically belonging rather to the turn of the 10th and 11th centuries.

The most interesting find that might be connected with the Rekomperk hillfort is, however, a hoard of bronze and other objects discovered close to the hillfort, on the boundary between the cadastral areas of Horné and Dolné Orešany. The hoard is one of the most important Late Avar find assemblages of its kind in the territory of Slovakia and Czechia. It was found in 2005 with a metal detector, and in 2006 the spot was subsequently examined by staff of the Institute of Archaeology of the Slovak Academy of Sciences. The hoard consists of 86 bronze, gilded, tinned and occasionally even silver objects; all are in good condition overall, although some are damaged or incomplete. Besides ornamental phalerae and the typical decorative mounts from horse harness and belts, there were also exceptional objects. The most important of them is a bronze cross of Byzantine type, which ranks among the rare Christian artefacts of the period of the Avar Khaganate. The arms of the cross widen and bear the symbols Alpha and Omega in relief. The edges and the central ring are decorated with a beaded pattern.
An identical specimen comes from the Avar cemetery of Lesencetomaj in Transdanubian Hungary.

For dating the hoard it is important that it comes almost exclusively from the final phase of the Avar Khaganate. Particularly significant is the presence of one tinned mount (no. 31), since the Carolingian style had probably already influenced the design of its decoration. On that basis it may be assumed that the hoard was deposited near Rekomperk during the Slavic–Avar conflicts of the time, which, with the defeat of the Avars by the armies of Charlemagne, subsequently led to the khaganate's demise. The hoard can therefore most likely be dated to the turn of the 8th and 9th centuries.
